strengths: Comprehensive empirical validation of attention low-rank structure across multiple model families, datasets, and layers with multiple converging metrics
Clever decomposition analysis (Section 4.3) isolating W^O anisotropy as the source of low-rank structure
Addresses a real practical problem (dead features) with a simple, effective solution that scales to 1M features
Extensive implementation details, ablations, and pseudo-code support reproducibility
Honest discussion of limitations and edge cases (JumpReLU failures, residual stream limitations) in appendices
Extension to multiple sparse dictionary learning methods (SAEs, Lorsa) demonstrates generalizability of the core insight
weaknesses: Causality between low-rank structure and dead features is observed but not mechanistically explained—no causal experiments with synthetic activations or theoretical analysis provided
Proposed method (PCA initialization) is incremental novelty—essentially applying existing PCsInit (Phan et al. 2025) to SAEs

Critical disconnect between improvements: reconstruction quality improves substantially but downstream Delta LM loss barely improves (Figure 6 note), questioning practical utility for interpretability

Significant limitations underemphasized in main text: (1) ASI fails with high-ℓ₀ warm-up schedules for JumpReLU SAEs (Appendix H), (2) produces more dead features than AuxK at extreme scale (1M features, Figure 7b), (3) minimal gains on high-rank activations like residual streams
Missing analysis of whether W^O anisotropy is inherent to multi-head attention or an avoidable design choice—no exploration of whether different W^O learning could reduce the low-rank structure
Hyperparameter d_init lacks principled selection guidance; claimed 'wide range' (256-2048 for 4096D) shows significant performance variation; unclear how to set for new architectures
Limited downstream validation: no experiments showing whether improved SAE reconstructions lead to better feature interpretability or other downstream benefits

strengths: Well-documented empirical phenomenon: Low-rank structure of attention outputs is systematically demonstrated across layers, model families, and datasets using three complementary metrics (intrinsic dimensionality, singular value decay, downstream loss recovery), with convincing evidence in Figures 1-2.

Clear mechanistic attribution: Section 4.3 effectively decomposes the variance contributions of head outputs Z versus projection matrix W_O, showing W_O is the primary source of low-rankness with intuitive superposition-based explanation.
Practical improvements at scale: ASI achieves substantial dead feature reduction (87%→<1%) across scales from 16K to 1M features, with thorough scaling experiments (Figure 7a).
Excellent reproducibility: Extensive appendices with implementation details, pseudo-code, hyperparameters, ablation studies, and clear experimental setup facilitate reproduction.
Generalization beyond SAEs: Demonstrates applicability to sparse replacement models (Lorsa), showing the approach generalizes beyond TopK SAEs.
weaknesses: Correlation does not establish causation: Figure 4 shows strong correlation between low intrinsic dimensionality and dead features, but the paper provides no mechanistic explanation for why low-rank geometry causes dead features. The acknowledged gap (Section 6: 'causal mechanism remains unclear') undermines the central claim that ASI addresses a fundamental geometric mismatch.

Confounded experimental results at scale: Major improvements in Figure 7a come from combining ASI with SparseAdam (which addresses stale momentum). The relative contribution of ASI versus optimizer choice at 1M features is unclear, making it impossible to isolate the method's true effect.

Severe method limitations in appendices: ASI fails for high-ℓ0 warm-up regimes (Appendix H) and shows minimal gains for residual streams (Appendix B.2). These are relegated to appendices despite being critical limitations that restrict applicability.

Incomplete guidance on applicability: Paper provides no quantitative threshold for when to apply ASI despite acknowledging singular value spectrum as an indicator. The vague guidance 'when spectrum decays rapidly in its tail' limits practical deployment.

Lack of theoretical grounding: No formal analysis of why random initialization fails specifically for low-rank data or why PCA-based initialization should solve the dead feature problem. Claims that low-rank structure is 'a key factor' in dead features are intuitive but unsubstantiated.

Remaining dead features at extreme scale: Figure 7b shows ASI produces more dead features than AuxK at 1M features. While Figure 7c argues these don't matter for reconstruction, this caveat directly contradicts the paper's primary claim of eliminating dead features.

Limited novelty of components: Prior work discusses low-rank attention (Section 2.1); Phan et al. (2025) already proposed PCA-based initialization. The connection to dead features is novel but insufficiently explained theoretically.

Incomplete experimental comparison: Generalization to other sparse dictionary methods shown only for Lorsa. Limited comparison with alternative dead feature mitigation approaches beyond AuxK. No comparison with other initialization schemes.

Hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed: Figure 5 shows significant sensitivity to D_init requiring grid search. The speculation (Appendix B.3) that small values fail due to subspace coverage is unvalidated.

Confounding by stale momentum: Appendix C identifies stale momentum as a separate dead feature cause addressed by SparseAdam. Large-scale improvements conflate ASI contributions with optimizer effects, obscuring what aspect of the method drives improvements.

strengths: Novel and robust empirical characterization of attention output low-rank structure (~60% intrinsic dimensionality) consistently demonstrated across three model families, three datasets, and multiple layers
Elegant mechanistic analysis in Section 4.3 decomposing variance contributions of head outputs versus output projection matrix, clearly attributing low-rankness to W^O anisotropy
Significant practical impact: reduces dead features from 87% to <1% at 1M features, addressing a real computational bottleneck in scaling SAEs
Thorough experimental validation with proper ablations, scaling laws (16K-1M features), and generalization to sparse replacement models (Lorsa)
Honest treatment of limitations and failure modes (high-ℓ₀ warm-up regimes, extreme-scale caveat) rather than overselling
Excellent presentation with clear writing, informative visualizations, extensive reproducible hyperparameters, and implementation pseudo-code
weaknesses: Causality between low-rank structure and dead features remains unclear—paper demonstrates strong correlation (Figure 4) but doesn't explain the mechanism, only acknowledging 'optimization dynamics or feature competition' without investigation
ASI effectiveness is context-dependent: fails with high-ℓ₀ warm-up schedules (Appendix H), requiring workarounds that undermine methodological elegance

Disentanglement of contributions unclear: ASI alone leaves ~40-50% dead features at 1M scale; SparseAdam reduces to <1%, suggesting SparseAdam provides most of the benefit—unclear how much ASI itself contributes
Limited applicability: method only works for low-rank activations; minimal gains on residual streams (Appendix B.2), suggesting this is a specialized rather than general technique
Caveat at extreme scales: ASI produces more dead features than AuxK at 1M features (Figure 7b), suggesting trade-offs not fully characterized
Limited methodological novelty: ASI is essentially 'compute PCA initialization' inspired directly by Phan et al. (2025); application to SAE dead features is incremental
Causality investigation is insufficient: paper shows correlation with dead features but doesn't deeply probe why—the proposed relationship may be coincidental or indirect

strengths: Novel and well-documented empirical finding: Low effective rank (~60%) of attention outputs demonstrated convincingly across 4 model families, multiple datasets, layers, and activation positions with three complementary metrics (effective rank, singular spectra, loss recovery)

Strong mechanistic analysis: Decomposition (Figure 4) clearly shows W^O's role in dimensionality reduction, with intuitive explanation of overlapping attention head subspaces supported by cross-model evidence

Practical solution with dramatic improvements: Active Subspace Initialization reduces dead features from 87% to <1% at 1M features, shows consistent gains across 16K-1M feature scales, and improves reconstruction quality (normalized MSE ~0.27 vs ~0.31)

Comprehensive experimental validation: Statistical significance testing (Welch's t-test, all p<1e-6), cross-layer/model/dataset evaluation (Tables 6-7), ablation studies (random vs active subspace), feature quality analysis (monosemanticity), and error analysis for stability

Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, pseudo-code provided, multiple experimental setups with 15-seed significance testing, clear descriptions of metrics, error analysis confirming 10M token stability
Method generalizes beyond SAEs: Successfully applied to Lorsa (sparse replacement models) with similar dead feature reductions, demonstrating broader applicability

Honest limitations discussion: Authors clearly acknowledge unresolved causal mechanism, edge cases with certain training schedules (high initial L0), performance at extreme scales, and appropriate use conditions
weaknesses: Causality unestablished: Paper demonstrates strong correlation between low effective rank and dead features (Figure 5, Tables 1-3) but provides no mechanistic explanation for *why* low-rank geometry causes dead features; missing experimental validation (e.g., artificially inducing low-rankness to test if dead features increase)

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Why does W^O become anisotropic during training? Is this fundamental or an artifact of specific choices? No analysis of whether this emerges during training or exists from initialization, despite claims it 'may reflect a more fundamental property'

ASI method limitations inadequately characterized: Fails with high initial L0 training schedules (Figures 15-16) requiring ad-hoc PCA preprocessing workaround; at extreme scales (1M features, Figure 8b) produces more dead features than AuxK baseline though reconstruction better; d_init hyperparameter lacks principled guidance

SparseAdam interaction analysis incomplete: Best results require ASI *and* SparseAdam, but contribution from each is unclear; SparseAdam addresses stale momentum (orthogonal concern) but relationship to low-rank structure unexplored; unclear if methods truly orthogonal or if interaction is significant

Limited characterization of ASI applicability: Yields minimal gains on near-full-rank activations (Figure 13), but systematic analysis missing; 'when to use ASI' acknowledged as unclear; boundaries of applicability (TopK yes, TopK-anneal no; JumpReLU conditional) not systematically mapped

Theoretical gaps: Overlapping subspaces explanation intuitive but not rigorously proven; no analysis of feature evolution during training or whether features drift from active subspace; missing connection between dimensionality and optimization landscape

Scope limitations: Only language models (vision transformers untested); models ≤8B parameters; limited multilingual testing; no analysis of potential architectural solutions (Section 6 mentions but doesn't explore)

Experimental inconsistencies: Figures 7-9 use 3 random seeds while significance testing uses 15 seeds; effect sizes inconsistently reported; computational cost of SVD initialization not discussed; some interpretation gaps for ablations

strengths: Novel and well-characterized empirical observation of low-rank attention outputs across multiple model families, datasets, and layers, demonstrated via complementary metrics (effective rank, singular decay, loss recovery)
Comprehensive experimental scope with 10M activation tokens per experiment, multiple random seeds, statistical significance testing, and detailed reproducibility information
Decomposition analysis (Section 4.4) effectively shows how the output projection matrix W^O contributes to rank collapse through anisotropic compression
Honest discussion of limitations, including unresolved causality, applicability constraints, and failure cases in appendices
Practical engineering contribution: reducing dead features from 87% to <1% in 1M-feature SAEs demonstrates scalable value
weaknesses: Critical: Causality between low-rank structure and dead features is explicitly unresolved—the paper acknowledges this but builds the entire solution narrative on this unproven assumption. No mechanism is established for why poor initialization specifically causes dead features despite billions of optimization steps

Limited novelty of proposed solution: Active Subspace Initialization is straightforward PCA-based weight initialization, directly extending Phan et al. (2025). For ICML, this requires deeper theoretical justification or substantial demonstrated impact, neither of which is provided

Method fails or provides marginal improvements in critical settings: (1) At 1M features (Figure 8b), ASI produces MORE dead features than AuxK (~50% vs ~20%), undermining headline claims; (2) JumpReLU and K-Anneal schedules (Appendix L) show complete failure when sparsity gradually increases; (3) Marginal gains on full-rank activations (Appendix J.2) contradict generality claims

No demonstration of improved interpretability: monosemanticity evaluation (Section N.1) finds no statistically significant differences in feature quality between ASI and TopK. Crucially, the paper does not show that reduced dead features translate to better circuit discovery, mechanistic insights, or interpretability

Unresolved mechanistic understanding: The paper lacks rigorous explanation for why low-rank structure causes dead features. The dimension bound in Section 4.4 (dim[∪_i span(O_i)] ≤ Σ dim[span(O_i)]) is trivial and always holds. Why doesn't SGD recover from poor initialization? Why is this specific to low-rank activations? These fundamental questions remain unanswered

Confounding factors with SparseAdam: Figure 8a shows ASI alone underperforms at scale; improvement is primarily from ASI+SparseAdam. The separate contributions are unclear, and stale momentum (Appendix M) may be the dominant factor, not subspace alignment

Experimental design issues: (1) Fixed d_init=768 across layers suboptimal (Table 6 shows Layer 7 still has 5308 dead features); (2) Outlier exclusion (>5σ) is ad-hoc; (3) Dead feature threshold (10M tokens) is borrowed without justification in this context; (4) Sensitivity to effective rank metric choice not explored

Limited scope: Method requires careful per-configuration tuning, fails with high-sparsity schedules, provides minimal benefit on full-rank activations. Claims of 'generalizability' are overstated given these constraints

strengths: Novel and rigorously demonstrated empirical finding that attention outputs are confined to surprisingly low-dimensional subspaces (~60% effective rank) across multiple model families, datasets, and layers with three complementary metrics providing convergent validity

Exceptional experimental rigor with statistical significance testing (Welch's t-test, p-values <10^-6 across 15 seeds), thorough ablation studies, and detailed error analysis (CV of 1.5×10^-4), enabling confident conclusions

Clear mechanistic insight via Figure 4's variance decomposition showing the output projection matrix W^O plays a key role in compressing multi-head activations, with intuitive explanation via overlapping subspace superposition

Practical and scalable solution (ASI) that dramatically reduces dead features from 87% to <1% at 1M features with zero additional computational overhead, and generalizes to other sparse dictionary methods (Lorsa, transcoders)
Excellent reproducibility with extensive hyperparameter documentation, pseudocode in appendices, multiple random seeds, and clear implementation details enabling straightforward reproduction
Well-structured presentation with effective visualizations and logical flow from phenomenon observation through problem identification to solution
weaknesses: Causality between low-rank structure and dead features remains unresolved despite strong correlation—paper cannot definitively explain why random initialization fails in low-rank spaces or rule out reverse causality, limiting conceptual depth

Method limitations inadequately emphasized: ASI produces more dead features than AuxK at extreme scales (Figure 8b), fails with high-ℓ₀ warm-up schedules (Appendix L), and requires orthogonal combination with SparseAdam for best results, suggesting it is not a complete solution

Limited theoretical understanding of why attention specifically exhibits low-rank structure while MLPs do not, despite both operating on full-rank residual streams; superposition explanation is intuitive but incomplete
Scope limited to language models only—claims of 'universality' lack validation on vision transformers, BERT-style encoders, or other architectures despite stating robustness across diverse settings

Underdeveloped analysis of practical and conceptual implications: paper does not explore whether low-rank structure is necessary for model function, investigate architectural improvements, or deeply examine downstream consequences for model behavior and efficiency

Feature quality analysis (monosemanticity in Appendix N.1) limited to 100 samples with no comparison of learned semantics between TopK and ASI, and hyperparameter d_init=768 chosen empirically without principled justification despite Figure 6 showing wide acceptable range

Hyperparameter sensitivity and practical requirements underspecified: SVD computation requires 10M tokens for stability (Appendix C), dead feature definition (10M token threshold) shows no sensitivity analysis, and scaling of SVD computational cost not thoroughly analyzed

Method shows activation-dependent efficacy with minimal gains on high-rank activations (residual streams, Appendix J.2), and fails under certain training schedules, limiting the scope of applicability claims
